sources.title: Fear and disruption for Ukraine's rail passengers as Russia escalates drone attacks
sources.excerpt: Ukrainians travelling by train are increasingly caught in the crosshairs of Russia's attacks.
sources.text: Fear and disruption for Ukraine's rail passengers as Russia escalates drone attacks. Ukraine's railways have kept the country running since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. But attacks are intensifying, with more than half of all strikes on locomotives since then occurring this year alone, according to the state-owned operator. Yuliia Ponomarenko, 27, a marketing specialist from Kharkiv, found her journey to Warsaw last month suddenly interrupted just short of the Ukraine-Poland frontier. "The border guards started running around and shouting "Run! Get out of the carriages! There's shelling!" A Russian drone had just hit a locomotive near the same border , and a special train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European dignitaries, had passed through minutes before. Passengers on Yuliia's train were kept waiting for six hours while the fire up ahead was put out and the line cleared, she says: "We were really lucky that we were delayed a little and it wasn't our train." She is among an increasing number of Ukrainian passengers facing disruption and long delays, as air raid alerts trigger emergency evacuations far from the battlegrounds of the east. In September alone, 5,831 trains had to be evacuated due to Russian drone attacks, state owned railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia told AFP news agency on Monday. This meant on average each day, 205 trains were stopped. It appears to be part of a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure, with two bridges attacked in Kyiv in the past few days and passengers of a metro train caught up in one of the strikes. Seventeen-year-old Anastasiia Ryvbalchenko has also experienced a narrow escape. She and her fellow passengers were forced to leave their train at 4am, towards the end of a long of a journey from Odesa to Kirovohrad on 16 September. "On my way to Odesa, there had been a lot of evacuations and now on my way back it was happening again," she says. "I was already thinking that if there was another evacuation, I just couldn't take it any more." An hour and a half later, as passengers waited in the dark, a drone struck nearby. "There was an extremely loud explosion and everyone started running into the woods," she said. It is not clear what the target was, and in this case the train was not damaged, but with further explosions lighting up the night sky, Anastasiia decided not to linger, continuing her journey on foot before being picked up by her parents. Anastassia's journey was more dramatic than most, but delays – some brief, others that last for hours – are now commonplace. Since Russian drones first started attacking moving passenger trains towards the end of 2025, the routine for passengers has become increasingly familiar: leave the train, scroll Telegram channels for updates on drone and missile launches, send messages to warn friends and family that the train is delayed. For a railway company proud of its record for punctuality, this year's disrupted schedule is posing a major challenge. "We used to say that that during times of war we performed better than some railways in Europe in regular times,"the head of rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, told us. "But now the life of our passengers and crew members is the utmost priority." Russia's defence ministry denies targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment. The dangers are very real. Attacks on Ukrzaliznytsia's rolling stock and stations have risen sharply. Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, almost 60% have been this year, according to statistics released by the company. Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year. "The latest wave of escalation and real war with railways is becoming extremely intense," said Pertsovskyi. "It's a combination of the deadly force of their shahed drones and precision that they achieve with cameras and mesh networks so they can hit moving targets." According to Pertsovskyi, some of Russia's most recent drones are equipped with AI tools and image recognition. Ukraine is understandably cagey about how it goes about confronting this increasingly sophisticated threat, but electronic methods to disrupt the drones' connectivity are high on the list. "Unfortunately, this is always a cat-and-mouse game," he said. We were given rare access to an underground bunker in Kyiv, dubbed – appropriately enough – the "Iron Command Centre", where railway staff monitor threats in real time. On one huge video screen, colour-coded passenger and freight trains could be seen making their way along the arteries of Ukraine's vast railway network. We watched as a red icon representing a drone appeared to loiter over Kyiv, practically above our heads at one point. Each drone had a 100km (62-mile) circle around it. Any passenger trains inside the circle would already have been evacuated, with customers not allowed to reboard until the train was outside the circle and the drone was still moving away. "Our mission is not to let our train or our crew members be in that immediate attack area," Pertsovskyi said. The company's precautions appear to have kept casualties low. Its figures for 2026 show that eight company employees have been killed, six of them when a ballistic missile struck a locomotive depot in Kyiv. During our visit to Iron Command, another air raid siren sounded in Kyiv. The city's main railway station, we were told, was being evacuated. On a later visit to the busy station, we found passengers waiting outside the main entrance or sheltering in underground passageways. Over the tannoy came news of steady stream of delays. Everyone knows the coming months could be among the most difficult yet. With winter not far off, Ukrzaliznytsia is already figuring out how to deal with evacuations when the outside temperature can reach -20C or below and snow is lying heavy on the ground. sources.title: Children among heavy casualties in Ukraine after Russian strikes
sources.excerpt: Windows shattered in the powerful blast in Pryluky, in the Chernigiv region, reducing one half of the five-storey building into a smoking pile of charred concrete and twisted metal
sources.text: Children among heavy casualties in Ukraine after Russian strikes. Windows shattered in the powerful blast in Pryluky, in the Chernigiv region, reducing one half of the five-storey building into a smoking pile of charred concrete and twisted metal. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said three of the 18 victims of the strike were just 12 months old while another was aged eight. Seven other children were among dozens wounded and one child was among 15 rescued, he wrote on social media, accusing Russia of knowingly striking “ordinary cities, ordinary life”. “The continued use of missiles against Ukraine, against our people, our children, is an absolutely deliberate choice of terror,” he said. “We were at home, sleeping,” Olena Sayun, a 40-year-old massage therapist, told AFP at the scene of the blast. “Our windows blew out. Thank God, we covered the child with our bodies. My husband got a few cuts on his back and I did too... “The child just had a nervous breakdown, got very scared. We immediately ran to the bathroom and then, while everything in the apartment was being blown apart, we stayed in there.” “All our kids are about the same age -- 10, 8, 14, 11,” she added. “They all played in our courtyard, on the playground, every single day. We knew them all very well.” The strike, which locals said happened at about 6.30 a.m. (0330 GMT), came after Mr. Zelenskyy on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) warned of a “massive” Russian attack, particularly targeting energy infrastructure. Two people were killed when missiles slammed into high-rise buildings in Dnipro and Kremenchuk in central Ukraine, while two others lost their lives in Oleksandriya, he added. In the capital, Kyiv, two people died in a fire caused by a strike in the densely populated Darnytskyi neighbourhood, the city’s mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Kyiv has come under increased attack in recent weeks as winter approaches, with air raid sirens wailing nearly constantly to warn of incoming Russian strikes. Worried residents hunkered down for the night in subway stations overnight, hauling duffel bags, sleeping mats and blankets. “We grabbed our things and came here, we live right next door,” Iryna Rybalchenko, who works in a bank, told AFP , sitting on the platform wrapped in a dark hoodie and surrounded by bags. “The whole of Kyiv is in a state of fear. We were stuck at work today and everyone — our group chats, our bosses — were messaging us to be careful.” Russia launched at least 50 missiles and 130 drones overnight against several regions including Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Poltava, Ukraine’s air force said. Mr. Zelenskyy, who called it “one of the most vile strikes” in the nearly five-year conflict, said some were shot down but ballistic missiles were “the greatest challenge” and new air defences were essential to help Ukraine defend itself. “I don’t see any military significance in this at all,” said Yuliia Shamrai, 31, who works in online marketing and lives near the stricken building in Pryluky. Asked why they had been hit, she added: “Just to break people, the civilian population that was peacefully sleeping.” Kyiv mayor Mr. Klitschko warned last week the capital should now be on a war footing after repeated strikes on bridges and energy infrastructure. Scheduled power cuts on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) plunged parts of Kyiv into darkness to ease the pressure on the battered grid, and generators cranked into life. The air force said on Wednesday (October 7, 2026) morning that it had intercepted five ballistic missiles, as well as 39 cruise missiles and over 100 drones. Ukraine has been struggling to down the new and fast-moving jet-powered drones, as well as the ballistic missiles that are harder to intercept. Concern has mounted about rising civilian casualties on both sides, as Ukraine also steps up its long-range attacks on Russian targets it says are vital to its war effort. “The children were absolutely terrified. Whenever there’s heavy shelling, we try to head underground,” Daria Medvedeva, 36, told AFP . Mr. Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s “just responses” to Russian strikes saw it hit two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions, as well as the Black Sea. sources.title: Russia Strikes Ukraine’s Flamingo Missile Facilities
sources.excerpt: The Russian troops’ advances are taking place on the day Putin turns 74. On Wednesday, the Russian Defense Ministry confirmed that its forces carried out multiple overnight strikes on Ukrainian military-industrial enterprises in several regions. RELATED: Putin Warns Against Seeking Russia’s Strategic Defeat In Kiev…
sources.text: Russia Strikes Ukraine’s Flamingo Missile Facilities. On Wednesday, the Russian Defense Ministry confirmed that its forces carried out multiple overnight strikes on Ukrainian military-industrial enterprises in several regions. In Kiev and the surrounding region, three enterprises used for the assembly and storage of FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles and FP-9 missiles as well as drone production and assembly were hit. The strikes also targeted facilities producing and storing components for FP-5 Flamingo missiles in Pryluky of the Chernihiv region and Lozova of the Kharkiv region; a drone component workshop in Oleksandriia of the Kirovohrad region; a rocket and space enterprise in Dnipro of the Dnipropetrovsk region used for the production, storage and supply of Flamingo missiles and drones; and some others. On the maritime front, a ship repair plant producing and storing naval drones and their components was struck in the port of Izmail, while a dry cargo ship delivering military supplies was hit in the port of Odesa. On Wednesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin turned 74, prompting numerous foreign leaders to congratulate him by phone. Putin, who was born in St. Petersburg in 1952 and has led Russia since 1999, held phone conversations with leaders from the post-Soviet space, including the Belarusian, Armenian, Kyrgyz and Tajik presidents. Chinese leader Xi Jinping had already congratulated him in advance on Tuesday, and Putin is expected to receive a phone call from U.S. President Donald Trump, who has expressed his willingness to address the possible outbreak of pneumonic plague in Siberia. The Kremlin also announced that, at the conclusion of his talks with his counterparts, Putin will chair a meeting of Russia’s Security Council amid an escalation of attacks between the Russian and Ukrainian armies. Following the 2020 constitutional reform, Putin will be eligible to run for president for a sixth time in 2030 and again in 2036.

sources.title: Ukraine war ‘a human rights catastrophe’ that must end, says Türk
sources.excerpt: The war in Ukraine is a human rights catastrophe that is “growing and intensifying by the week” and threatening an even greater disaster across the region, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said on Friday.
sources.text: Ukraine war ‘a human rights catastrophe’ that must end, says Türk. The war in Ukraine is a human rights catastrophe that is “growing and intensifying by the week” and threatening an even greater disaster across the region, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said on Friday. Addressing the Human Rights Council in Geneva, Mr. Türk said his office had verified some 15,280 civilians killed and injured in Ukraine during the first eight months of this year – on average more than 400 every week , and 55 per cent more than in the same period in 2025. “The full-scale invasion unleashed by the Russian Federation is killing and injuring hundreds of people every week, as frontlines barely move, ” he said, noting that apartment buildings, schools, medical centres, railways and shops had been hit in recent attacks. The UN rights chief said a recent report by his office had found “ shocking levels of sexual violence against civilians and prisoners of war ”. Of more than 1,000 cases documented, 89 per cent were attributed to Russian authorities and 11 per cent to Ukraine . Most victims were men, particularly in places of detention, but women and children were also affected, primarily in occupied territory. “This is just one terrible manifestation of the cruelty that has come to define this war. Alongside peace, there must be accountability ,” he said. Mr. Türk said people across Ukraine were living in constant dread, with air raid alerts in Kyiv active for 33 hours during one 48-hour period earlier this week . Near the frontlines, the use of aerial glide bombs by the Russian Federation in the Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia regions killed and injured nearly 2,500 civilians in the first eight months of the year; 62 per cent more than in the same period last year. “Ukraine is a laboratory for drone warfare,” he said, calling for urgent international action to deal with the carnage caused by these weapons around the world. Attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial property have increased sharply, he said, and Russian strikes on supermarkets and food companies are already causing temporary shortages of vegetables and dairy products in some areas. “As winter approaches, Ukrainians fear the worst is yet to come.” An estimated 2,000 people are trapped in Oleshky without running water, electricity or gas, he added. Civilian casualties in the Russian Federation have also reportedly increased, Mr. Türk said, though his Office has been unable to fully verify reports as it has not been granted access. He urged the Russian leadership to “consider what this war is doing to their own society”, which he said was sinking into fear, denial and a militarized economy “that puts death and destruction ahead of healthcare and education ”. Mr. Türk also said he was alarmed by human rights violations linked to the presence of fighters from third countries. His staff have interviewed prisoners of war from 36 countries held by Ukraine, many of whom said they had been deceived into joining Russian forces . Mr. Türk called for confidence-building measures based on human rights to rebuild momentum towards negotiations. These could include an agreement to end attacks on economic targets and energy infrastructure, local ceasefires on the frontlines, enabling civilians to leave – and a full exchange of prisoners of war. “To the international community, and particularly states with influence, I say: please take urgent action to push for a negotiated peace now, before this tragedy becomes even worse ,” he said.

sources.title: Ukraine Builds Airless Wheels to Keep Ground Robots Moving After Battlefield Damage
sources.excerpt: Ukrainian firms Print&Live UA and iSCALE 3D unveiled airless wheels for unmanned ground vehicles, enabling continued mobility after tire damage.
sources.text: Ukraine Builds Airless Wheels to Keep Ground Robots Moving After Battlefield Damage. Ukrainian companies Print&Live UA and iSCALE 3D have developed lightweight airless wheels for unmanned ground vehicles operating on the front line. Militarnyi reported the development on October 7, citing the companies behind the project. According to the outlet, the wheels are designed specifically for ground robotic systems, where conventional pneumatic tires remain vulnerable to punctures and battlefield debris. We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field. The new design eliminates the need for compressed air, allowing a wheel to remain functional after damage that could disable a conventional tire, Militarnyi added. The developers also focused on reducing the wheel's weight, an important factor for smaller robotic platforms with limited payload and battery capacity. According to Militarnyi, the project combines Print&Live UA’s experience in additive manufacturing with iSCALE 3D’s work on large-format 3D printing. The technology allows components with complex internal structures to be manufactured without using traditional tire-production tooling. Airless wheels use a flexible structural body rather than air pressure to support the vehicle’s weight and absorb impacts. For military ground robots, this can reduce the risk of losing mobility after running over fragments, nails, or other sharp objects common on the battlefield. Militarnyi noted that such components are particularly relevant for unmanned ground vehicles used for logistics, evacuation, and other missions in areas where recovering a disabled platform can expose personnel to additional risk.

sources.title: Map Shows Ukraine’s September Gains as Russian Casualties Hit 2026 High
sources.excerpt: Russia suffered its highest monthly losses of the year in September but gained no territory in return, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), whose latest map outlines the state of the ...
sources.text: Map Shows Ukraine’s September Gains as Russian Casualties Hit 2026 High. Russia suffered its highest monthly losses of the year in September but gained no territory in return, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) , whose latest map outlines the state of the frontline. Ukraine’s armed forces said on Thursday that Russia had suffered 46,000 casualties last month, while the Washington, D.C.-based think tank gave its assessment of how the battlefield has shifted over the last six months. This has coincided with a Ukrainian counteroffensive, "Operation Vivaldi," in the Lyman sector of the Donetsk oblast, which has thwarted Moscow’s attempts to capture the "Fortress Belt" of cities critical to holding the Donbas region. High Russian troop losses for negligible territorial gains add pressure on President Vladimir Putin amid speculation about a widespread mobilization to replenish troops. Newsweek reached out to the Russian defense ministry for comment. It is tricky to ascertain losses in the Ukraine war, with both sides tight-lipped about casualty figures. Moscow has not updated its death toll from the 6,000 it revealed in the first year of the war. But evidence suggests Russian losses are rising amid minimal battlefield gains. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said last month that Russia had over 40,000 casualties per month, referring to those who have been killed and injured. This was up from the 30,000-a-month figure he gave in June, the same month in which the British government said intelligence indicated nearly 500,000 Russian soldiers had been killed, as it assessed that the Russian military is “going backwards on the battlefield.” The September figure from Ukraine’s armed forces, released Thursday, was its highest monthly tally of the year—up from 42,860 in July and a marked increase from January’s 32,980. Meanwhile, the ISW said it was unclear how much territory Russian forces lost the same month due to the uncertainty about when Ukrainian forces liberated territory near Lyman. “Russian forces continue to sustain significant personnel losses while achieving extremely limited or even net negative territorial gains,” the think tank said, noting how Russia's recruits are not enough to replace the losses. The Kremlin has repeatedly denied it planned a widespread mobilization. The ISW also said that between March and September, Russian troops lost almost 115 square miles of territory. Operation Vivaldi started in early summer and has liberated at least 147 square kilometers (56 square miles), according to Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps commander, Andriy Biletskyi, who has touted the use of drones, robots and deception as contributing to the gains. As its map shows, the ISW said it had evidence that Russian forces seized 175.54 square kilometers (67 square miles) last month but lost 256.35 square kilometers (98 square miles) of territory in September, for a total loss of 80.81 square kilometers (30 square miles). Meanwhile, the Vivaldi operation near Lyman could complicate Russia's offensive toward the fortress-belt city of Sloviansk, which has worried Russian military bloggers who offer an unvarnished view of Moscow’s war effort. The ISW cited the military bloggers' concerns that the Ukrainian counteroffensive may stop Russian plans to assault the Fortress Belt cities from the front. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Robinson and Sam Wilson.

sources.title: Russia Just Got Smacked with a New Crisis: 650 Drones Were Sent to Moscow by Ukraine and Putin Faces a Growing Crisis
sources.excerpt: Ukraine hit an oil depot that fuels Moscow's three biggest airports as six hundred fifty drones approached the capital, its mayor said.
sources.text: Russia Just Got Smacked with a New Crisis: 650 Drones Were Sent to Moscow by Ukraine and Putin Faces a Growing Crisis. Overnight on Monday into Tuesday, Ukraine launched a major drone attack on the Moscow area, one that, among other targets, hit the Volodarskaya Line Production and Dispatch Station (LPDS), a major oil depot that supplies fuel in the area. According to the Kyiv Post, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said on Telegram that 650 drones approached Moscow overnight and claimed air defenses intercepted most of them. Ukraine Cruise Missile. Image Credit: Government of Ukraine. Ukraine War TOS-2. Image Credit: X Screenshot. Moscow Oblast Governor Andrei Vorobyov claimed that 105 drones were intercepted and that one person was killed. About the Depot Transnefteprodukt, part of Russia’s state-owned Transneft oil pipeline company, owns the Volodarskaya Line Production and Dispatch Station. It supplies fuel to Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Sheremetyevo, Moscow’s three largest airports, Kyiv Post said. Last week, Ukraine struck another large Russian oil hub, the Samara LDPS in Samara Oblast. Ukraine has been stepping up attacks on oil infrastructure in Russia in recent weeks. Ukraine War Map. Image Credit: Creative Commons. Neptune Missile. Image Credit: Government of Ukraine. Russia has 32 oil refineries, most of which have been hit at some point during the war. Half the Capacity? Earlier this week, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry claimed it has knocked out more than half of Russia’s refining capacity, as reported by the Associated Press. After attacks on refineries in Moscow, Yaroslavl, Ust-Luga, Perm, Saratov, and Syzran, Ukraine said it knocked out 51 percent of Russia’s capacity, although the AP could not confirm the figure. Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara attributed the 51 percent figure to Ukraine’s intelligence services, General Staff and the Defense Ministry, and called the lost capacity “a significant blow to the enemy’s economy, to its ability to carry out aggression and supply its troop groupings.” “They started attacking oil refineries and openly declared the goal of damaging our economy,” Russian President Vladimir Putin stated at the Valdai Club address last week, the AP said. Putin, however, claimed the attacks had knocked out only about 1 percent of Russia’s GDP. Oil From South Korea The Guardian reported Tuesday that Russia has turned to an unlikely place for its oil needs: South Korea. The newspaper’s analysis found that Russia received 150,000 tons of fuel in July and August, some carried by sanctioned vessels. The oil left South Korean ports on seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s Far Eastern coast, according to the Guardian’s investigation. The U.K. and the European Union have sanctioned three of the vessels. South Korea is nominally supportive of Ukraine in the war, while North Korea is supportive of Russia, including sending soldiers and weapons to the frontline. However, The Guardian reported that South Korea has sought to find “balance” between its support for Ukraine and its desire for better relations with Russia. South Korea has sent armor, helmets, and other items to Ukraine during the war, along with financial support. But South Korea has not provided weapons, as part of its longstanding policy of not providing weapons to foreign wars. Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), told the Guardian that it was “shocking” that sanctioned tankers had brought oil from South Korea to Russia, which “undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.” No Oil Truce President Donald Trump, in recent weeks, has been pushing Russia and Ukraine to stop attacking each other’s oil refineries, in light of the skyrocketing price of diesel. At one point, in mid-September, Trump even declared that the two sides had agreed to halt such attacks. However, as with most of Trump’s attempts to end or de-escalate the war, this did not succeed, and both countries later denied reaching any such agreement. A potential truce was discussed around the time of the United Nations General Assembly, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky telling Trump he would support it. However, days later, Putin made it clear that Russia was not interested in any such agreement. “We are told: ‘Let them stop striking your refineries, and you will stop striking their ships.’ It is simply ridiculous,” the Russian president said last week during his address at the Valdai political forum in Moscow, as reported by Al Jazeera. About the Author: Stephen Silver Stephen Silver is an award-winning journalist, essayist, and film critic, and contributor to the Philadelphia Inquirer, the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, Broad Street Review, and Splice Today. The co-founder of the Philadelphia Film Critics Circle, Stephen lives in suburban Philadelphia with his wife and two sons. For over a decade, Stephen has authored thousands of articles that focus on politics, national security, technology, and the economy. Follow him on X (formerly Twitter) at @StephenSilver, and subscribe to his Substack newsletter.

sources.title: Ukraine Frontline Update: Fighting Across Key Sectors on October 7
sources.excerpt: Latest frontline update from Ukraine on October 7, covering fighting near Sumy, Kharkov, Krasny Liman, Dobropolye, Gulyaypole, Zaporozhye and key advances.
sources.text: Ukraine Frontline Update: Fighting Across Key Sectors on October 7. Latest frontline update from Ukraine on October 7, covering fighting near Sumy, Kharkov, Krasny Liman, Dobropolye, Gulyaypole, Zaporozhye and key advances. The Russian Armed Forces continue their special military operation in Ukraine. As of October 7, the situation along the line of contact is as follows. Russian aircraft, artillery and UAV units are carrying out strikes near Sumy, Kiyanitsa, Boyaro-Lezhachaya, Barilovka and Rudnevka. Small-arms fighting is taking place near Kiyanitsa and Khoten in the Sumy district. In the Shostka district, Russian forces have advanced through forest belts near Korenek. The opposing side is moving reserves, artillery and multiple-launch rocket systems toward Sumy. Intense fighting continues around Chuguyev, Veliky Burluk, Chernoglazovka, Dementiyevka, Novoselovka, Belashi, Cherkasskaya Lozovaya, Goryanoye and Kupino. Russian forces have advanced near Tokarevka. On the Volchansk and Veliky Burluk sectors, Russian assault groups have moved forward in the areas of Varvarovka, Reznikovo, Lobanovka, Kotovka and Annopolye. Fighting also continues for Ukrainian positions and supply routes north and east of Kupyansk, as well as near Kupyansk-Uzlovoy. Heavy fighting is under way in and around Krasny Liman, including on the approaches to the city. The opposing side is bringing in reinforcements and attempting to hold its positions there. Russian units continue to apply pressure from the direction of Zarechnoye and the surrounding forested areas. Russian troops are advancing along the railway north of Sergeyevka and expanding their area of control on the eastern approaches to the settlement. Fighting continues inside Dobropolye itself, where Russian forces are taking up new positions in the southern part of the city. Russian forces are expanding their bridgehead for a further advance toward Novonikolayevka. The Russian army has taken Golubkova.

sources.text: Front line. A front line is the point at which the most advanced tactical combat units intersect, creating an area of potential or actual conflict. Leaders have often fought at the front lines either purposefully or due to a collapse in battle formation. While a calculated risk, fighting on the front has in instances reduced communication, and heightened morale. The front is in direct contrast to the rear, which is the position furthest from conflict.
